title: Vectors, one-forms and tensor algebra
scope: Multilinear algebra at a single point and differentiation in inertial (constant-basis) coordinates: index notation and the summation convention; four-vectors versus their components; bases, dual bases and transformation matrices; one-forms, their pairing with vectors and their stacked-surface picture; gradients; tensors as multilinear maps with type, components, tensor products, contraction and the transformation law; covariance of tensor equations; symmetry, bracket notation and the Levi-Civita symbol; the flat-spacetime metric as a map between vectors and one-forms with raising and lowering of indices; and gradients, divergences and the d'Alembertian of tensor fields in Minkowski coordinates. Position-dependent bases, manifolds, densities and exterior forms are left to later domains.

concepts.title: Index notation and index ranges
concepts.summary: Spacetime components are labelled by indices: Greek letters run over 0 to 3 (time and space) and Latin letters over 1 to 3 (space only), and a prime or bar on an index marks components in a second frame. Superscripts are labels, not powers.
concepts.notes: Includes the Newtonian Cartesian tensor notation that d'Inverno sets up (indices 1-3 moved with the Kronecker delta) so Newtonian and relativistic equations can be compared symbol by symbol. Books differ on which alphabet is spatial; check the convention before reading.

concepts.title: Einstein summation convention
concepts.summary: When an index letter appears once as a superscript and once as a subscript in the same term, a sum over all its values is understood and the sigma is dropped. Sums of this kind are exactly matrix multiplication written out in components.
concepts.notes: Example: the pairing of Lambda with its inverse, a sum over a shared index, is the row-times-column rule, so index expressions can be checked as matrix products (Schutz ch2). Schutz Appendix A writes every sum explicitly and is a useful decoder. d'Inverno states the rule for any repeated index, while Schutz and Gifted Amateur require one index up and one down.

concepts.title: Free and dummy indices
concepts.summary: A free index appears once in every term and turns an equation into one equation per value; it must carry the same name in every term. A dummy index is summed over, so its letter is arbitrary and may be renamed to any unused letter of the same range.
concepts.notes: Relabelling dummy indices is the key step in deriving the basis-vector transformation law. Independent sums need distinct dummy letters (Schutz Exercise 3.1 contrasts a correct double sum with an illegal single one).

concepts.title: Kronecker delta
concepts.summary: The Kronecker delta equals 1 when its two indices are equal and 0 otherwise; as a matrix it is the identity. With one index up and one down it is a genuine (1,1) tensor whose components are the same in every basis, and contracting with it simply renames an index.
concepts.notes: It appears as the product of a transformation matrix with its inverse and as the value of basis one-forms on basis vectors. Gifted Amateur Exercise 4.2 asks whether the all-up and all-down versions are tensors: in general coordinates they are not.

concepts.title: Four-vector
concepts.summary: A four-vector is an arrow in spacetime, such as the displacement between two events, whose four components change from one inertial frame to another by the same Lorentz transformation that acts on coordinate differences. Four-vectors add and scale component by component, forming a four-dimensional real vector space.
concepts.notes: The displacement vector between events is the prototype; d'Inverno promotes the tangent-vector transformation law to a definition of a contravariant vector in general coordinates. Physical four-vectors (four-velocity, four-momentum) are taught in special-relativity; this concept covers the algebraic object. Later reinterpreted as a (1,0) tensor, a linear function of one-forms.

concepts.title: Basis vectors
aliases: basis vectors of an inertial frame
concepts.summary: A basis is a set of four reference vectors e_0 to e_3 such that every four-vector is a unique linear combination of them. In its own inertial frame each basis vector points along one coordinate axis, and its components are a column of the identity matrix; the lower index names which vector is meant, not a component.

names: basis vectors of an inertial frame

merged_from: basis vectors of an inertial frame
concepts.notes: The dot products of basis vectors give the metric components. The index on a basis vector is written low so that the summation convention applies in A^alpha e_alpha. Basis vectors of different frames are different vectors.

concepts.title: Components of a vector
concepts.summary: The components of a vector are the numbers A^mu in the expansion A = A^mu e_mu on a chosen basis. They depend on the whole basis, not only on the basis vector they multiply, so changing any member of the basis can change every component.
concepts.notes: Schutz Appendix A shows with a skew basis in the plane (e_1 = e_x, e_2 = e_y - e_x) that a nonorthogonal basis is as valid as an orthonormal one, but components can then no longer be read off as dot products with the basis vectors.

concepts.title: Inner product, norm and orthogonality
concepts.summary: An inner product is a symmetric bilinear rule giving a number for each pair of vectors; in relativity it is indefinite, so the squared norm of a nonzero vector can be positive, negative or zero. Two vectors are orthogonal when their inner product vanishes, which means a null vector is orthogonal to itself.
concepts.notes: Schutz Appendix A takes |A| = |A.A|^(1/2) so the norm stays real; d'Inverno defines the angle between non-null vectors with absolute values of norms. The Minkowski scalar product of four-vectors and the timelike, null and spacelike classification are taught in special-relativity.

concepts.title: Orthonormal basis
concepts.summary: An orthonormal basis has mutually orthogonal vectors each of unit magnitude, so the metric components in it are those of the identity (Euclidean) or of eta (Lorentzian). Hats on indices mark components in such a basis, for example the unit polar vectors e_r-hat and e_theta-hat = e_theta / r.
concepts.notes: Convenient but never required. Orthonormal frames on curved spacetime (tetrads, vielbeins) belong to differential-forms-and-frames.

concepts.title: Geometric object versus components
concepts.summary: A vector or tensor is a single frame-independent object; its components are just the numbers it produces on a particular basis. Changing frame changes the components but never the object, because the new components and new basis vectors recombine into the same sum.
concepts.notes: Schutz enforces this through notation (bars go on indices, never on the vector). He uses the number-flux vector to show that the prerelativistic 3-flux was frame dependent because it was only part of one invariant object.

concepts.title: Coordinate independence of physical laws
concepts.summary: Coordinates are arbitrary labels with no physical meaning, so physical laws should be statements about geometric objects that hold in every coordinate system. Tensors are the tool for this: equations between them and fully contracted scalars do not depend on how coordinates are laid down.

names: coordinate independence as the motivation for tensors in physics

merged_from: coordinate independence as the motivation for tensors in physics
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur uses Newton's second law in a rotating frame: its components acquire centrifugal and Coriolis terms although the relation between the two arrows is unchanged. d'Inverno cites this as Einstein's motivation for tensors. The physical principle of general covariance belongs to equivalence-principle.

concepts.title: Coordinate transformation matrix
concepts.summary: The transformation matrix Lambda^{mu'}_nu = partial x^{mu'} / partial x^nu collects the first derivatives of new coordinates with respect to old ones at a point; its inverse is partial x^mu / partial x^{nu'}, and their product is the Kronecker delta. For inertial frames it is the constant Lorentz matrix.

names: transformation matrices for vectors and one-forms

merged_from: transformation matrices for vectors and one-forms
concepts.notes: Index placement (which index is primed) tells which of the two matrices is meant. In general coordinates both matrices depend on position (Schutz ch5). Lorentz boost matrices happen to be symmetric, which hides the row-versus-column distinction in special relativity.

concepts.title: Active versus passive transformation
concepts.summary: A passive transformation relabels the same points and objects with new coordinates, so components change while nothing physical moves. An active transformation keeps the coordinates and moves the points, dragging tensors along, and its formulas can look identical to a passive change while meaning something different.
concepts.notes: Coleman's image, quoted in Gifted Amateur: under a passive change the criminal stays put but uses an alias, under an active change he has an alibi elsewhere. The tensor transformation law is passive. The active view underlies push-forwards and Lie derivatives, and a diffeomorphism is its most general smooth form (used in the hole argument).

concepts.title: Transformation law for vector components
concepts.summary: Under a change of frame or coordinates, vector components transform with the forward matrix, A^{mu'} = (partial x^{mu'} / partial x^nu) A^nu. Any set of four quantities that obeys this rule is the component set of a vector.

names: tangent components through the chain rule

concepts.notes: The finite position array x^mu fails this test in general coordinates, while the differentials dx^mu pass it.

concepts.title: Transformation law for basis vectors
concepts.summary: Basis vectors transform with the inverse of the matrix used for components, e_{mu'} = Lambda^nu_{mu'} e_nu. This inverse pattern is forced by requiring the vector A^mu e_mu itself to be unchanged by the frame change.

names: transformation of basis vectors and basis 1-forms

merged_from: transformation of basis vectors and basis 1-forms
concepts.notes: Derived by substituting both laws into A^mu e_mu and relabelling dummy indices. Basis one-forms transform the other way, like vector components, which Gifted Amateur summarizes with all four rules in one table (eqn 4.37).

concepts.title: Scalar invariant
concepts.summary: A scalar invariant is a single number whose value is the same in every frame or coordinate system, making it a tensor of type (0,0); a scalar field assigns such a number to each event. Fully contracting tensors always produces scalars, so a scalar can be computed in whichever frame is easiest.
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur uses the demand that contractions be invariant to derive the one-form transformation law.

concepts.title: One-form
concepts.summary: A one-form is a linear map that takes a vector and returns a real number. One-forms at a point add and scale like vectors, so they form a vector space of the same dimension, the dual space; their components carry lower indices.
concepts.notes: d'Inverno defines a covariant vector through its transformation law, promoted from the gradient. Gifted Amateur compares one-forms to bras dual to kets. The Gifted Amateur "linear slot machine for vectors" is this concept. p-forms and the exterior algebra belong to differential-forms-and-frames; the cotangent space of a manifold belongs to manifolds-and-metrics.

concepts.title: Contraction of a one-form with a vector
aliases: vectors as linear functions of one-forms
concepts.summary: Feeding a vector to a one-form gives the number p(V) = p_mu V^mu, a sum with all plus signs that needs no metric. It is the same in every frame because the forward and inverse transformation matrices cancel, and it lets a vector be read equally as a linear function of one-forms, so the two spaces are dual to each other.

names: vectors as linear functions of one-forms
pairing of a 1-form with a vector
contraction of a 1-form with a vector

merged_from: contraction of a 1-form with a vector
pairing of a 1-form with a vector
vectors as linear functions of one-forms
concepts.notes: Contrast with the scalar product of two vectors, which needs the metric as a third object. Schutz's "circular reasoning?" interlude explains that mutual definition of vectors and one-forms is duality, not circularity.

concepts.title: One-form as a stack of surfaces
concepts.summary: A one-form at a point can be pictured as a family of evenly spaced parallel surfaces; its value on a vector is the number of surfaces the arrow crosses. Closer spacing means a larger one-form, and the picture needs no metric.

names: picture of a one-form as stacked surfaces

merged_from: picture of a one-form as stacked surfaces
concepts.notes: Justified through the gradient and contour maps, and made physical by surfaces of constant phase of a wave. Gifted Amateur links the picture to reciprocal-lattice vectors labelling crystal planes.

concepts.title: Dual basis
concepts.summary: Given basis vectors e_nu, the dual basis consists of the one-forms omega^mu defined by omega^mu(e_nu) = delta^mu_nu. In this basis any one-form expands as p = p_mu omega^mu with p_mu = p(e_mu), which is what makes p(A) = p_mu A^mu hold.
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur boxes the duality relation as the single most important rule for manipulating tensors. In a Lorentz frame the dual basis one-forms are the gradients of the coordinates, dx^mu.

concepts.title: Transformation law for one-form components
concepts.summary: One-form components transform with the inverse matrix, p_{mu'} = (partial x^nu / partial x^{mu'}) p_nu, the same way basis vectors transform. This opposite pattern to vector components is exactly what keeps the contraction p_mu A^mu invariant.
concepts.notes: Obtained either by evaluating the one-form on the new basis vectors or by demanding invariance of the contraction; confirmed for the gradient by the chain rule.

concepts.title: Contravariant and covariant components
concepts.summary: Traditionally, quantities that transform like coordinate differentials are called contravariant and carry upper indices, while those that transform like gradients (and like basis vectors) are covariant and carry lower indices. Geometrically, in a skewed basis the upper components come from parallel decomposition and the lower ones from dot products with the basis vectors, and they coincide only in an orthonormal Euclidean basis.
concepts.notes: A common source of confusion: Gifted Amateur avoids the terms, reserving "covariant" for "transforms properly", and Schutz calls them old-fashioned because they mix up a change of basis with a change of components. Coordinates carry upper indices even though x^mu are not vector components.

concepts.title: Gradient one-form
concepts.summary: The gradient of a scalar field phi is the one-form d(phi) whose value on a vector V is the rate of change of phi along V; its components in any coordinates are the partial derivatives partial phi / partial x^mu. The chain rule makes these components transform like a one-form, so the gradient is the archetypal one-form.

names: directional derivative of a scalar along a world line
differential of a function as a 1-form

merged_from: directional derivative of a scalar along a world line
differential of a function as a 1-form
concepts.notes: Motivated by following a world line through a scalar field: d phi / d tau is the gradient evaluated on the four-velocity. It annihilates every vector tangent to a level surface. The index-free exterior derivative of a function is covered in differential-forms-and-frames.

concepts.title: Comma notation for partial derivatives
concepts.summary: A comma before an index denotes a partial derivative with respect to that coordinate, phi_{,alpha} = partial phi / partial x^alpha. The index sits low because the result transforms as a one-form component.
concepts.notes: Examples: x^alpha_{,beta} = delta^alpha_beta and T^alpha_{beta,gamma}. The companion semicolon notation for covariant derivatives is taught with the covariant derivative in connection-and-parallel-transport.

concepts.title: Normal one-form
aliases: gradient as normal to a surface
concepts.summary: A normal one-form to a surface is one that vanishes on every vector tangent to the surface; the gradient of f is normal to the surfaces f = constant. Unlike a normal vector it needs no metric, and it is fixed only up to an overall factor.
concepts.notes: Used in Schutz ch4 to describe hypersurfaces and to compute fluxes across them.

concepts.title: Multilinearity
concepts.summary: A function of several arguments is multilinear if it is linear in each argument when the others are held fixed: scaling one input scales the output, and splitting one input into a sum splits the output. This property is what lets every tensor be evaluated by expanding its inputs on a basis.

concepts.title: Tensor
concepts.summary: A tensor of type (M, N) at a point is a multilinear machine that takes M one-forms and N vectors and returns a real number. Its value does not depend on any frame; only its components do.

names: linear slot machine picture of tensors

merged_from: linear slot machine picture of tensors
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur's "linear slot machine" is this definition, and filling only some slots gives a lower-rank object. d'Inverno instead defines tensors by their transformation law (see tensor-transformation-law) and sketches the multilinear-map definition only briefly. Tensor fields on manifolds belong to manifolds-and-metrics.

concepts.title: Type (valence) of a tensor
concepts.summary: The type or valence (M, N) counts a tensor's one-form slots (upper indices) and vector slots (lower indices); a mixed tensor has both. Vectors are (1,0), one-forms (0,1), the metric (0,2), and a number results only when the slots of a tensor are all filled.
concepts.notes: Rank-two tensors come as (2,0), (1,1) or (0,2), each with a 4x4 component array. Bold index-free symbols hide the valence, one motivation for abstract indices. The legacy course notes that tensor rank is not matrix rank.

concepts.title: Tensor product
concepts.summary: The tensor (outer) product of two tensors is the tensor whose slots are the first factor's slots followed by the second's, with value equal to the product of the factors' values: (p x q)(A, B) = p(A) q(B). It adds the types and is not commutative, because slot order matters.
concepts.notes: In components it multiplies every component of one factor by every component of the other, A^a B^b = C^{ab}. Its appearance in the Lieber cartoon of d'Inverno ch1 is its only mention there.

concepts.title: Components of a tensor
concepts.summary: The components of a tensor are its values when basis one-forms are put into its upper slots and basis vectors into its lower slots. Multiplying the components by tensor products of the matching basis elements and summing rebuilds the tensor, so the 16 products omega^alpha x omega^beta form a basis for (0,2) tensors.

names: component extraction by inserting basis vectors and 1-forms
component extraction by inserting basis objects
component extraction by inserting basis vectors

merged_from: component extraction by inserting basis objects
component extraction by inserting basis vectors
component extraction by inserting basis vectors and 1-forms
concepts.notes: The same recipe extracts components from index-free expressions such as the covariant derivative and the curvature operator in Gifted Amateur chs 34-35.

concepts.title: Tensor transformation law
concepts.summary: Tensor components transform with one forward matrix partial x'/partial x for each upper index and one inverse matrix partial x/partial x' for each lower index, with no extra terms. Coordinate-based treatments take this rule as the definition of a tensor.

names: tensor transformation law of the metric

merged_from: tensor transformation law of the metric
concepts.notes: Example: the metric transforms with two inverse Jacobian factors, which keeps ds^2 unchanged (Gifted Amateur ch5); for (0,2) tensors in matrix form f' = Lambda^T f Lambda. Connection coefficients fail this test, which is why they are not tensors.

concepts.title: Covariance of tensor equations
aliases: true in one frame, true in all
concepts.summary: If two tensors of the same type are equal in one coordinate system at a point, they are equal in every coordinate system, since their difference has all components zero and stays zero under the homogeneous transformation law. So an equation with matching tensor types and free indices on both sides can be proved in the most convenient frame and trusted everywhere.

names: valid tensor equation versus component relation

merged_from: valid tensor equation versus component relation
concepts.notes: A tensor equation must match valence on both sides, so the (1,3) Riemann tensor cannot equal the (2,0) stress-energy tensor. Contrast: a relation between components in two specific coordinate systems (Schutz Eq. 8.22) need not balance its primed indices and is not a tensor equation. A theory is covariant when its equations keep their form under the relevant coordinate changes. General covariance as a physical principle belongs to equivalence-principle.

concepts.title: Tensor contraction
concepts.summary: Contraction sets one upper index equal to one lower index and sums, turning a type (M, N) tensor into a type (M-1, N-1) tensor; the result is again a tensor because the paired transformation matrices cancel. The trace of a (1,1) tensor, S^mu_mu, is the simplest example and is a scalar.
concepts.notes: Contracting two lower indices is not allowed without the metric, so the trace of a (0,2) tensor needs the inverse metric. Gifted Amateur writes the trace with the tensor's letter in italic, except that g is the metric determinant.

concepts.title: Permissible tensor operations
aliases: addition and scalar multiplication of tensors
concepts.summary: Some operations on tensor components always produce another tensor: adding tensors of the same type at the same point, multiplying by a scalar, taking outer products, contracting an upper with a lower index, and (in curved spacetime) covariant differentiation. Building expressions only from these makes type checking routine.

names: addition and scalar multiplication of tensors

merged_from: addition and scalar multiplication of tensors
concepts.notes: Schutz ch6 gives the list as a numbered review; d'Inverno checks tensor character through the transformation law.

concepts.title: Quotient theorem
concepts.summary: If an array of numbers, contracted with an arbitrary tensor, always gives a tensor, then the array is itself the component set of a tensor. It is a quick way to establish tensor character without checking the transformation law directly.
concepts.notes: d'Inverno uses it to conclude that R^a_bcd is a (1,3) tensor.

concepts.title: Symmetric and antisymmetric tensors
concepts.summary: A two-slot tensor is symmetric if swapping its inputs leaves the output unchanged, T_ab = T_ba, and antisymmetric if the swap flips the sign; either property survives any change of coordinates. Every (0,2) tensor splits uniquely into a symmetric and an antisymmetric part, which in n dimensions have n(n+1)/2 and n(n-1)/2 independent components (10 and 6 in spacetime).

names: independent components of a symmetric tensor

merged_from: independent components of a symmetric tensor
concepts.notes: Totally (anti)symmetric tensors have the property for every pair of slots of the same kind; swapping two slots is the transpose operation. The metric and the stress-energy tensor are symmetric; the Faraday tensor is antisymmetric. The count of 10 components explains why the linearized gravitational field is more complicated than the electromagnetic potential.

concepts.title: Symmetrization and antisymmetrization brackets
concepts.summary: Round brackets around indices mean the average over all orderings of those indices, T_(ab) = (T_ab + T_ba)/2, and square brackets mean the signed average, T_[ab] = (T_ab - T_ba)/2, each with weight 1/r! for r indices. Vertical bars inside brackets exclude indices from the operation.
concepts.notes: Symmetrizing leaves symmetric tensors unchanged and kills antisymmetric ones. The three-index form is needed for the cyclic identity of the Riemann tensor.

concepts.title: Levi-Civita symbol
concepts.summary: The Levi-Civita symbol epsilon_{abcd} is totally antisymmetric: it equals +1 for an even permutation of 0123, -1 for an odd permutation, and 0 if any index repeats. It writes determinants as signed sums over permutations and gives the components of the volume form in an orthonormal basis.

names: Levi-Civita tensor sign convention in Minkowski spacetime

merged_from: Levi-Civita tensor sign convention in Minkowski spacetime
concepts.notes: Sign convention trap: with epsilon_0123 = +1 and signature (-+++), raising all four indices gives epsilon^0123 = -1. d'Inverno stresses that the symbol with the same numbers in every chart is not a tensor but a tensor density (weight +1 up, -1 down); densities belong to manifolds-and-metrics and the volume form and Hodge star to differential-forms-and-frames.

concepts.title: Generalized Kronecker delta
concepts.summary: The generalized Kronecker delta with k upper and k lower indices is +1 if the upper indices are distinct and an even permutation of the lower ones, -1 for an odd permutation, and 0 otherwise. It equals the determinant of the k-by-k array of ordinary deltas, the antisymmetrized product of deltas.
concepts.notes: Used in Gifted Amateur ch32 for the pairing of basis p-forms with basis p-vectors, and in d'Inverno ch7 for subspace volume elements.

concepts.title: Epsilon-delta contraction identity
concepts.summary: The product of an upper and a lower Levi-Civita symbol equals the generalized Kronecker delta with the same indices, and contracting successive index pairs gives lower-order deltas with factorial factors (in four dimensions: 1, 2, 3! and 4!). With a Lorentzian metric, an extra factor (-1)^s appears when both symbols come from the metric volume tensor.

names: generalized Kronecker delta and epsilon-epsilon identity

merged_from: generalized Kronecker delta and epsilon-epsilon identity
concepts.notes: The three-dimensional version reproduces the familiar vector identities for double cross products.

concepts.title: Metric tensor of flat spacetime
concepts.summary: The scalar product is itself a symmetric (0,2) tensor g: it takes two vectors and returns A.B = g_{mu nu} A^mu B^nu. Its components in any basis are the dot products of the basis vectors, g_{mu nu} = e_mu . e_nu, which in every inertial frame are eta_{mu nu} = diag(-1, 1, 1, 1).

names: metric components as basis-vector dot products
metric as dot products of basis vectors

merged_from: metric as dot products of basis vectors
metric components as basis-vector dot products
concepts.notes: The same tensor has other components in other bases (the Euclidean metric in polar coordinates has g_rr = 1, g_theta theta = r^2). The metric tensor field on a curved manifold, its inverse and determinant belong to manifolds-and-metrics.

concepts.title: Metric as a map from vectors to one-forms
concepts.summary: Filling one slot of the metric with a vector V leaves a one-form g(V, _) whose value on any A is V.A; because the metric is nondegenerate, this correspondence between vectors and one-forms is one-to-one and invertible. It is the metric's fundamental role: without it, vectors and one-forms are separate objects with no scalar product.

names: metric as a map from vectors to one-forms
metric as a map from vectors to 1-forms

merged_from: metric as a map from vectors to 1-forms
metric as a map from vectors to one-forms
concepts.notes: Schutz contrasts this with nonmetric settings such as classical and quantum phase space, where vectors and one-forms exist but no identification between them is preferred. Choosing a metric is added structure.

concepts.title: Raising and lowering indices
concepts.summary: Contracting a tensor index with the metric g_{mu nu} lowers it, V_mu = g_{mu nu} V^nu, and contracting with the inverse metric g^{mu nu} raises it; the results are treated as components of the same geometric object and keep its letter. In an inertial frame, moving a time index flips the component's sign and moving a spatial index leaves it unchanged.

names: raising and lowering indices with the metric

merged_from: raising and lowering indices with the metric
concepts.notes: Raising one index of the metric gives the Kronecker delta, so the inverse metric is the metric with both indices up. Confusion traps: the left-to-right order of mixed indices matters (X_a^b differs from X^b_a); with non-diagonal metrics such as Eddington-Finkelstein, g^{mu mu} is not 1/g_{mu mu} and raising mixes components (Gifted Amateur ch26). In linearized gravity indices are moved with eta (gravitational-waves).

concepts.title: Inner product and magnitude of one-forms
concepts.summary: The squared magnitude of a one-form is defined as that of its associated vector and is computed directly with the inverse metric, eta^{mu nu} p_mu p_nu; the inner product of two one-forms follows the same way. A one-form is called timelike, spacelike or null according to whether this magnitude is negative, positive or zero.

concepts.title: Vector gradient
concepts.summary: Raising the index of the gradient one-form gives the gradient vector, with inertial-frame components (-phi_{,t}, phi_{,x}, phi_{,y}, phi_{,z}); it is orthogonal to every vector tangent to a surface of constant phi. The elementary "grad" of vector calculus is this vector, which is why it secretly depends on the metric.

names: inverse metric and the vector gradient

merged_from: inverse metric and the vector gradient
concepts.notes: Even in Euclidean space the vector and one-form gradients have different components outside Cartesian coordinates: in polar coordinates the vector gradient has components (d phi/dr, r^-2 d phi/d theta) (Schutz ch5). Gifted Amateur criticizes the old grad construction for its index mismatch.

concepts.title: Momentum one-form
concepts.summary: The momentum of a particle is naturally a one-form p_mu, since a Lagrangian gives lower-index components p_mu = partial L / partial (dx^mu / d tau). Fed an observer's four-velocity it returns minus the energy that observer measures, E = -p(u).
concepts.notes: The minus sign comes from the (-+++) signature. Observer-measured energy itself is taught in special-relativity.

concepts.title: Wave-vector one-form
concepts.summary: For a wave, the one-form k whose surfaces are the surfaces of constant phase has components k_mu = (-omega, k); contracting it with a displacement vector counts the phase difference between the two events. It is the most physical instance of the stacked-surfaces picture.
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur first computes the phase with a four-vector and a dot product, then shows the one-form route needs no metric.

concepts.title: Constant basis in an inertial frame
aliases: constant basis in a Lorentz frame
concepts.summary: In an inertial (Lorentz) frame the basis vectors and basis one-forms are the same at every event, so differentiating a tensor field only differentiates its components. This fails in curvilinear coordinates and in curved spacetime, and dropping it is the entry point to the covariant derivative.

names: constant basis in a Lorentz frame

merged_from: constant basis in a Lorentz frame

concepts.title: Gradient of a tensor field
aliases: derivative of a tensor in a Lorentz frame
concepts.summary: The gradient of a type (M, N) tensor field is a type (M, N+1) tensor nabla T whose extra vector slot, filled with U, gives the rate of change of T along U. In inertial coordinates its components are just partial derivatives of the components, such as T^alpha_{beta,gamma}.

names: directional derivative of a tensor along a vector

merged_from: directional derivative of a tensor along a vector
concepts.notes: Derived by differentiating along a world line and removing the tangent vector. Gifted Amateur pictures it as the change in the tensor's output from the base to the tip of the inserted vector. In curved spacetime it becomes the covariant derivative (connection-and-parallel-transport).

concepts.title: Four-divergence
concepts.summary: The four-divergence of a vector field is the contraction of its gradient, V^a_{,a} = partial_t V^0 + partial_x V^x + partial_y V^y + partial_z V^z, a frame-independent scalar in special relativity. Local conservation laws take the form "four-divergence equals zero".
concepts.notes: Divergence of higher-rank tensors (contracting the derivative slot with an upper slot) follows the same pattern; the curved-space version is in connection-and-parallel-transport.

concepts.title: d'Alembertian operator
concepts.summary: The d'Alembertian is the Lorentz-invariant second-order operator box = eta^{mu nu} partial_mu partial_nu, equal to -partial_t^2 + nabla^2 in signature (-+++) (with the opposite overall sign in (+---)). Setting box f = 0 gives the wave equation, and for static fields it reduces to the Laplacian.
concepts.notes: Appears in linearized gravity, electromagnetism and the Klein-Gordon equation. The sign depends on signature convention: d'Inverno's (+---) gives partial_t^2 - nabla^2.

concepts.title: Index-free notation
concepts.summary: Index-free notation writes tensors as whole objects with empty slots, such as S( , , , ) or nabla_u v, rather than as arrays of components. Coordinate independence is then built in and the geometric meaning is visible, though long contractions are clumsier.
concepts.notes: Gifted Amateur argues for it against "death by indices"; d'Inverno weighs it against the index approach and chooses indices for practicality.

concepts.title: Abstract index notation
concepts.summary: In abstract index notation, index letters record the type and slot structure of a tensor (for example T^{ab}_c) without referring to any basis, so index manipulations are automatically coordinate-free; a separate alphabet is reserved for actual components.
concepts.notes: Mentioned but not adopted by Gifted Amateur and d'Inverno (who recommends Wald). Penrose's related diagrammatic notation draws tensors as shapes with one line per index, with joined lines as contractions (Gifted Amateur Exercise 31.7).

out_of_scope_candidates.name: symmetry of pure boost matrices
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Symmetric boost matrices and the rotation hidden in composed boosts are properties of Lorentz transformations.

out_of_scope_candidates.name: invariant versus coordinate-dependent quantities
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Observer agreement on the interval versus frame-dependent simultaneity and lengths is taught with special relativity (Schutz ch1).

out_of_scope_candidates.name: metric tensor in polar coordinates
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Metric components in polar coordinates are the curvilinear-coordinate rehearsal.

out_of_scope_candidates.name: gradient of a vector field
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Gradient of a vector field built with a connection (Gifted Amateur ch34).

out_of_scope_candidates.name: nabla_mu as a directional label
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Notation for the covariant derivative direction.

out_of_scope_candidates.name: coordinate-free, mixed and coordinate notation
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Levels of covariant-derivative notation (nabla_u v, (nabla_u v)^mu, v^alpha_;mu).

out_of_scope_candidates.name: flux as contraction of one-form with vector
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Flux of a conserved current across a hypersurface as a contraction; applies one-form-vector-contraction.

out_of_scope_candidates.name: projection operator
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Projector onto a spacelike hypersurface inducing the spatial metric (Gifted Amateur Exercise 30.7); the four-velocity projector is in matter-and-stress-energy.

out_of_scope_candidates.name: determinant of a rank-2 tensor via alternating symbols
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Determinant as a scalar density of weight 2 via alternating symbols; tensor densities.

out_of_scope_candidates.name: field of scalars
out_of_scope_candidates.note: Field of scalars for a vector space.
